{{Short description|Contour integral involving a product of gamma functions}}
In mathematics, a '''Barnes integral''' or '''[[Hjalmar Mellin|Mellin]]&ndash;Barnes integral''' is a [[contour integral]] involving a product of [[gamma function]]s. They were introduced by {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Ernest William Barnes|first=Ernest William |last=Barnes|year1=1908|year2=1910}}. They are closely related to [[generalized hypergeometric series]].

The integral is usually taken along a contour which is a deformation of the imaginary axis passing to the right of all poles of factors of the form Γ(''a''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''s'') and to the left of all poles of factors of the form Γ(''a''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''s'').

==Hypergeometric series==
The [[hypergeometric function]] is given as a Barnes integral {{harv|Barnes|1908}} by 

:<math>{}_2F_1(a,b;c;z) =\frac{\Gamma(c)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)} \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{-i\infty}^{i\infty} \frac{\Gamma(a+s)\Gamma(b+s)\Gamma(-s)}{\Gamma(c+s)}(-z)^s\,ds,</math>

see also {{harv|Andrews|Askey|Roy|1999|loc=Theorem 2.4.1}}. This equality can be obtained by moving the contour to the right while picking up the [[Residue (complex analysis)|residues]] at ''s'' = 0, 1, 2, ... . for <math>z\ll 1</math>, and by analytic continuation elsewhere. Given proper convergence conditions, one can relate more general Barnes' integrals and [[generalized hypergeometric function]]s <sub>''p''</sub>''F''<sub>''q''</sub> in a similar way {{harv|Slater|1966}}.

==Barnes lemmas==
The first Barnes lemma {{harv|Barnes|1908}} states

:<math>\frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{-i\infty}^{i\infty} \Gamma(a+s)\Gamma(b+s)\Gamma(c-s)\Gamma(d-s)ds
=\frac{\Gamma(a+c)\Gamma(a+d)\Gamma(b+c)\Gamma(b+d)}{\Gamma(a+b+c+d)}.
</math>

This is an analogue of [[Hypergeometric function#Special values at z = 1|Gauss's <sub>2</sub>''F''<sub>1</sub> summation formula]], and also an extension of [[Euler integral|Euler's beta integral]].  The integral in it is sometimes called '''Barnes's beta integral'''. 

The second Barnes lemma {{harv|Barnes|1910}} states

:<math>\frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{-i\infty}^{i\infty} \frac{\Gamma(a+s)\Gamma(b+s)\Gamma(c+s)\Gamma(1-d-s)\Gamma(-s)}{\Gamma(e+s)}ds</math>

:<math>=\frac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)\Gamma(c)\Gamma(1-d+a)\Gamma(1-d+b)\Gamma(1-d+c)}{\Gamma(e-a)\Gamma(e-b)\Gamma(e-c)}
</math>

where ''e'' = ''a''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''b''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''c''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''d''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1.  This is an analogue of [[Saalschütz's summation formula]].

==q-Barnes integrals==
There are analogues of Barnes integrals for [[basic hypergeometric series]], and many of the other results can also be extended to this case {{harv|Gasper|Rahman|2004|loc=chapter 4}}.
